transcript:
Meeting header
Date/Time: 2026-02-11 15:00 PST / 2026-02-11T23:00:00Z
Duration: ~55 minutes
Attendees: Alex Martinez (Redwood AE), Priya Shah (Redwood SE), Michael Chen (CTO, Concord HealthTech), Sara Lopez (Head of MLOps), David Patel (Infra Eng)

Summary (auto): Technical deep dive comparing Redwood hosted API vs Dedicated (reserved) and private deployment options. Focus areas: runtime perf (latency/throughput), KV cache behavior, batching strategies, quantization tradeoffs, noisy neighbor/isolation, VPC/on-prem constraints and throughput guarantees. Next steps: share pricing, benchmarks, schedule on-prem feasibility.

Transcript:
[00:00] Alex: Hi everyone, thanks for joining, I think we have about 55 minutes. Quick intro - I'm Alex, AE, and Priya our SE will lead the technical sections.
[00:15] Michael: Thanks, Alex. Michael here. We're excited to dig in — main ask is we need predictable latency for patient-facing summaries and throughput during peak hours, and we also have strict data residency and SOC2 needs.
[00:30] Priya: Great. Today we'll cover hosted vs dedicated vs private: how latency and throughput look, what the KV cache and batching do to tail latency, and options around quantization and on-prem. I'll open with a quick architecture sketch.
[00:45] Priya: So for hosted, it's multi-tenant. You hit the Redwood API, requests are routed and served from our shared clusters. For Dedicated you get reserved GPU pools, your own isolated tenants, and for Private we can run within your VPC or on-prem with a private control plane.
[01:10] Sara: Quick question — when you say isolated for Dedicated, is that tenant-level isolation only, or do you guarantee physical GPU exclusivity?
[01:20] Priya: Good q. Dedicated means reserved capacity — in most configs it's pools of GPUs dedicated to your account. It's not necessarily single-tenant physical host forever, but we provision that capacity only for you which eliminates noisy neighbor issues typical of shared pools. For absolute physical isolation (air-gapped) we have Private on-prem deployments.
[01:40] David: And network wise — for Private, can we do VPC peering or do you require an IPSEC/VPN? We have strict VPC controls.
[01:50] Priya: We support VPC peering and private connectivity. For on-prem we do an appliance-style deployment and we can work with your network team. We'll follow up with the detailed network diagram.
[02:10] Alex: Ok, let's move into runtime perf. Priya, can you walk through latency vs throughput tradeoffs and KV cache?
[02:20] Priya: Sure. Two big knobs: batching and KV caching. Batching improves throughput but adds queuing latency. The runtime uses continuous batching — it will accumulate small requests up to a latency SLO or batch size limit. For short completion use cases (single-shot summarize), small batches or no batching keeps p50/p90 low. For high throughput streaming workloads, batching reduces per-token cost significantly.
[02:50] Michael: What's typical p95 numbers for hosted vs dedicated on, say, a 2k token completion?
[03:00] Priya: For hosted, p95 is variable depending on region and current load — typical numbers we see are 180-350 ms per token at steady-state for 2k, but there's more tail due to multi-tenant scheduling. With Dedicated, because of reserved pools and predictable batching behavior, p95 tightens — we often see 120-220 ms per token. Quantization and model size change those numbers.
[03:30] Sara: When you say per token ms, are you measuring wall-clock server time or including network hop? We need end-to-end SLO.
[03:40] Priya: Good call — those numbers are server-side generation times only. Network/RTT will add to client-perceived latency. For E2E p95 in the same region you're usually adding 15-40 ms for network.
[03:55] David: Noisy neighbor — we've seen big swings on other providers. How deterministic is Dedicated throughput? If we reserve, say, 4 A100-equivalent GPUs, do we get guaranteed qps?
[04:10] Priya: Dedicated gives you prioritized capacity and autoscaling policies you configure. We provide throughput estimates and committed capacity. For strict guarantees we offer Reserved Capacity SLAs in contracts — the exact qps per GPU depends on model, sequence length, and quantization. We'll provide a throughput table.
[04:30] Michael: Can you share an example? Like for a 30 token output workload, what's qps on 4 GPUs?
[04:40] Priya: Rough example: for a 30-token average completion on a 4xA100 pool, with batching tuned, you might get 600-1,200 qps depending on model architecture and sequence lengths. We'll include exact benchmark numbers in the sheet.
[04:55] Sara: That range is wide — can we run a short POC benchmark with our prompts?
[05:05] Alex: Absolutely, that's standard. Priya will share the benchmark workbooks and we'll schedule a run using your sample traffic.
[05:15] Priya: Now KV cache — this is a big lever for chat-style workloads. Our runtime supports KV caching so repeated prefixes avoid re-computing encoder states. For long conversation contexts this reduces compute dramatically and lowers latency.
[05:35] Michael: Does KV cache persist across requests, or is it per-session? We have multi-shard user routing concerns.
[05:45] Priya: Cache is managed per-conversation and can be persisted in-memory on the serving node or backed to a fast KV store. For Dedicated you can configure larger in-memory caches. For Hosted we do per-tenant caching but eviction is based on memory pressure and global policies — so persistence guarantees are weaker unless you use Dedicated or Private where you can tune cache sizes.
[06:10] David: If the cache is in-memory on the node, what's the failover path? If a request goes to a different node without the cache, do you recompute and pay the latency?
[06:20] Priya: Yes — that's the fallback. We have sticky routing options and affinity to improve cache locality. For strict cache locality we recommend Dedicated with affinity enabled or Private deployment where you control routing.
[06:35] Michael: Quantization — how much does int8 or int4 impact latency and quality?
[06:45] Priya: Quantization trims both memory and compute. Int8 often gives 1.2-1.8x speedups on inference kernels with minimal quality drop for many workloads. Int4 can provide larger gains but requires careful validation — you might see more quality regressions on some tasks. For customers sensitive to hallucinations, we recommend int8 plus targeted evaluation. We'll share model-specific quant profiles.
[07:10] Sara: Do you support mixed precision and dynamic kernel selection?
[07:15] Priya: Yes; the runtime dynamically selects kernels and can run mixed precision paths depending on model and sequence length. The kernel selector tries to optimize for latency or throughput based on policy.
[07:30] Alex: On the topic of batching and tail latency — we offer latency-first routing where batches are cut off early to meet SLOs. That reduces throughput but improves tail. Any customer seen this tradeoff and have preferences?
[07:45] Michael: For patient-facing features we prefer latency-first. For background batch jobs we can favor throughput.
[07:52] Priya: Exactly. You'll be able to configure per-route policies: e.g., route A uses latency-first with batch size cap 8 and max wait 8ms, route B uses throughput-first batch size 128.
[08:05] David: For hosting in the EU region we have additional compliance and residency needs. How do dedicated pools map to regions? Can we have a dedicated pool only in eu-west-1?
[08:18] Priya: Yes, you can pin Dedicated pools to regions; for Private we'd deploy into your VPC or on-prem regionally. We also support key management integrations (KMS/HSM) for Private and Dedicated.
[08:35] Sara: Speaking of KMS, what's the model for key control in Hosted? Do we manage customer keys?
[08:40] Priya: Hosted supports bring-your-own-key (BYOK) via cloud KMS in some plans, but for full customer-controlled HSM we recommend Private. We'll include the security matrix in the docs.
[08:55] Michael: Any runbooks around noisy neighbor detection and mitigation? If we see a sudden tail spike, how do we quickly isolate?
[09:05] Priya: We log per-route metrics and have tracing hooks. For Dedicated, noisy neighbor effects are minimal because your pool is reserved. For hosted, we have autoscaling and fallback policies (route to different region, fallback to smaller model). If you need, we can enable alerting thresholds to trigger failovers.
[09:25] Sara: About failover — is there automated fallback to a smaller model? How do you preserve prompt fidelity there?
[09:34] Priya: We support automatic fallback chains where if the primary model latency or errors exceed thresholds we route to a compatible smaller variant and add metadata to responses indicating fallback. This reduces availability risk but you should test quality regression for critical flows.
[09:50] David: For on-prem, what hardware do you support? We standardize on DGX-like nodes or can adapt?
[09:58] Priya: We support common GPU classes (A100, H100 equivalents) and can work with your existing infra; our ops package documents minimum specs. For air-gapped we provide an installer and runtime that runs without outbound control plane in some configs.
[10:15] Michael: Latency guarantees in contract — can you commit to p95 numbers for dedicated pools?
[10:22] Alex: We have SLA tiers. For strict commitments we do reserved capacity contracts with defined p95 targets for server-side generation times. Those are backed by credits. We'll have legal and SRE draft language for a term sheet.
[10:40] Priya: One more note on KV cache sizing: we often see a 3-8x compute reduction for chat histories when KV cache hit rates are high. So latency and cost both improve. Your workload profiles will determine required RAM for cache.
[10:58] Sara: The cache persistence option you mentioned — can we snapshot and reload between restarts for stateful recovery?
[11:06] Priya: In Private and Dedicated you can configure a fast checkpoint store to persist cache to a local NVMe or fast network KV store to minimize cold-start degradation. Hosted offers ephemeral caching; persistent cache is a Dedicated/Private option.
[11:25] Michael: Ok, switching to batching — how do you recommend we tune for our workload? We have mixed traffic: short real-time summaries and nightly bulk generation of reports.
[11:36] Priya: Split workloads by route. Real-time route: low batch size, aggressive latency cap. Bulk job route: higher batch size, throughput-first. We also recommend separate model variants for bulk to use quantized or trimmed checkpoint for cost efficiency.
[11:55] David: When you change batch config or kernel selection, do you need model restarts or is it dynamic?
[12:02] Priya: Many parameters are dynamic but some lower-level kernel choices may require warm restarts. We plan deployments to avoid disruption and provide canary rollouts.
[12:15] (crosstalk)
[12:20] Michael: Any tips for designing prompts to improve caching/hit rates?
[12:25] Priya: Stable prefixes help. If you can canonicalize turn-level metadata or avoid per-request unique tokens in prefix, the KV cache hits improve. Also chunking long contexts into summary tokens can reduce recomputation.
[12:45] Sara: For the POC, can you run bench on Dedicated and Hosted so we can compare both under our load?
[12:50] Alex: Yes — Priya will run both with your prompts and we'll include configs for cache settings, batching, and quantization.
[12:58] Priya: We'll also include noise tests — artificially spike other tenants in hosted to show tail behavior vs dedicated.
[13:10] Michael: About monitoring — what observability do you expose? Token-level latency, per-route breakdowns?
[13:18] Priya: Redwood Console shows token-level cost and latency breakdowns, per-model dashboards, traces, and rollout metrics. You can hook into logs and metrics via Prometheus, and we provide exported traces for deep dives.
[13:35] David: For security reviews, we need SOC2 Type 2 evidence, encryption in flight at rest, audit logs, RBAC and SSO. Are those available for Dedicated?
[13:46] Priya: Yes. SOC2, audit logs, RBAC, SSO/SAML are available. For Private on-prem you get maximum control. We will attach the security pack and compliance sheet.
[14:00] Michael: Any gotchas for on-prem where our network has strict egress rules?
[14:06] Priya: We'll support air-gapped installation; some telemetry and auto-update features can be disabled. There is an ops overhead for fully air-gapped installs.
[14:20] Sara: Cost — what's the delta between Hosted pay-as-you-go and Dedicated reserved? We expect Dedicated is cheaper per token at scale but with commit.
[14:29] Alex: Exactly — Dedicated reduces unit cost via reserved GPU amortization. We'll send pricing bands; usually at committed levels you see meaningful savings.
[14:40] Michael: Ok sounds good. Any final technical notes?
[14:45] Priya: Two things: one, rolling quantization and model variant testing is critical — we recommend a small internal eval set. Two, plan cache sizing and affinity for chat workloads to avoid cold-start latency.
[15:00] Michael: Great. Let's recap next steps.
[15:05] Alex: Recap: we'll send pricing and reserved capacity options, Priya will share benchmark sheet and proposed test configs, customer will provide sample prompts and peak qps, and we'll schedule on-prem feasibility call.
[15:20] Michael: Thanks all. Good session.

(End of transcript)
